title: Orthogonal Junk: Gradient-Orthogonality Data Selection for Continual Pre-Training on Low-Quality Data

raw.stage1:
**Purpose:**  
The contribution aims to mitigate "brain rot," a specific form of capability degradation in LLMs caused by continual pre-training on low-quality social media data. No prior paper explicitly addresses this problem. While papers like [14] and [15] discuss catastrophic forgetting in continual learning, and [24] mentions catastrophic forgetting during domain adaptation, these focus on different phenomena (forgetting prior tasks or general reasoning capabilities) rather than degradation from low-quality data during continual pre-training. Papers like [11] and [12] address harmful content filtering or multilingual continual pre-training but do not target the specific issue of "brain rot" caused by low-quality social media data. Thus, the purpose is **uncovered**.  

**Mechanism:**  
The mechanism, Orthogonal Junk, involves a three-stage pipeline: computing anchor gradients from diverse capability benchmarks, scoring candidate samples by gradient orthogonality to those anchors, and using pool-weighted sampling to balance selection quality with diversity. Papers [18], [19], [24], and [27] discuss orthogonal gradient projection methods for continual learning or domain adaptation, but these focus on avoiding catastrophic forgetting or improving new task learning, not data selection. Paper [24] mentions gradient orthogonality for data selection but does not use anchor gradients or pool-weighted sampling. Papers like [4], [6], and [9] discuss balancing quality and diversity in data selection but do not use gradient orthogonality as a scoring mechanism. Thus, the mechanism is **uncovered**.  

**Evaluation:**  
The evaluation design uses standard benchmarks (RULER, ARC-Challenge) and measures performance improvements in long-context understanding and reasoning. Papers like [6], [9], and [13] use similar evaluation designs, combining benchmark-based performance metrics with gradient-based data selection methods. For example, [6] evaluates diverse instruction data selection using benchmarks, and [9] measures reasoning improvements with gradient alignment-based data selection. The specific benchmarks differ, but the evaluation design (benchmark-based validation of data selection methods) is substantively equivalent. Thus, the evaluation is **covered**.  

**Domain:**  
The domain is continual pre-training and LLM data selection. Papers like [2], [4], [6], [9], [13], and [24] all operate in the same general area of LLM data selection for pre-training or fine-tuning. While the specific focus on mitigating "brain rot" is unique, the domain itself (continual pre-training and data selection for LLMs) is well-covered by prior work. Thus, the domain is **covered**.
